documents.abstract: The study identifies the organizational factors that contribute to the development of burnout syndrome among professionals in the health, education, and telecommunications sectors in the Baixada Fluminense region, part of the metropolitan area of the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. This is an exploratory study with a qualitative approach. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews with seven professionals, and the empirical material was analyzed following Bardin’s content analysis procedures. The results indicate that factors such as work overload, micromanagement, lack of autonomy, and a high-pressure environment are determinants of emotional exhaustion, reduced productivity, and high staff turnover. Participants identified work overload and the accumulation of duties, limited autonomy, pressure related to goals and deadlines, and insufficient organizational support as the main organizational factors. Several interviewees reported difficulties disconnecting from work, interference with their personal lives, fatigue, stress, and a perceived deterioration in emotional well-being. Some also reported having considered leaving their jobs. Most participants did not identify specific organizational actions aimed at preventing burnout, although one divergent experience involving institutional emotional health initiatives was observed. It is concluded that the absence of effective organizational strategies for burnout prevention perpetuates the vulnerability of these workers, reinforcing the urgent need for more localized and effective occupational health policies.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technological innovations of the twenty-first century, fundamentally changing the way individuals learn, work, communicate, and solve complex problems. Although AI has become a prominent component of modern society only in recent decades, its conceptual foundations extend back several centuries through philosophical discussions concerning human intelligence, logical reasoning, and mechanical computation. The evolution of Artificial Intelligence represents a multidisciplinary journey involving computer science, mathematics, cognitive psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy, engineering, statistics, and data science. Continuous advancements in computational power, algorithmic development, data availability, and digital infrastructure have enabled AI to evolve from theoretical concepts into intelligent systems capable of performing tasks that traditionally required human intelligence. The earliest ideas related to artificial intelligence originated long before the invention of computers. Ancient civilizations imagined intelligent machines capable of mimicking human behaviour through myths, literature, and mechanical inventions. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, philosophers and mathematicians such as René Descartes, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, and George Boole contributed foundational concepts related to logic, reasoning, symbolic representation, and mathematical computation. Their work laid the intellectual groundwork for the development of computational systems capable of representing knowledge and making logical decisions.The modern evolution of Artificial Intelligence began during the twentieth century with the rapid advancement of computing technologies. In the 1930s and 1940s, significant progress in mathematical logic and computer science established the theoretical basis for intelligent machines. Alan Turing introduced the concept of a universal computing machine and later proposed the famous Turing Test, which examined whether a machine could demonstrate behaviour indistinguishable from that of a human being. Turing's pioneering contributions remain fundamental to contemporary AI research because they established that machines could potentially perform intelligent reasoning through computational processes. A major milestone occurred in 1956 during the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and Nathaniel Rochester. This conference formally introduced the term "Artificial Intelligence" and established AI as an independent scientific discipline. Researchers believed that human intelligence could be represented computationally and that machines could eventually perform reasoning, learning, language understanding, and problem-solving. The Dartmouth Conference inspired widespread academic interest and initiated decades of intensive research into intelligent computing systems.The period between the late 1950s and early 1970s is often referred to as the early development phase of Artificial Intelligence. During this era, researchers developed symbolic AI methods that emphasized logical reasoning, rule-based systems, theorem proving, and problem-solving algorithms. Early AI programmes successfully solved mathematical problems, played strategic games such as chess, and demonstrated limited natural language capabilities. Optimism surrounding AI research increased substantially as scientists believed that general human-level intelligence could be achieved within a relatively short period. However, limitations in computing power, data availability, memory capacity, and algorithmic efficiency restricted further progress. During the 1970s and 1980s, Artificial Intelligence experienced periods commonly known as the "AI Winters," characterized by reduced research funding, slower technological progress, and diminished public expectations. Many ambitious predictions regarding human-level machine intelligence proved unrealistic because available computing resources and algorithms were insufficient to support increasingly complex AI applications. Despite these challenges, important research continued in knowledge representation, expert systems, machine learning, robotics, and computational reasoning. Expert systems became particularly successful by capturing specialized human knowledge through rule-based decision-making frameworks that supported medical diagnosis, engineering design, financial analysis, and industrial management.The late 1980s and 1990s marked the gradual resurgence of Artificial Intelligence through the development of machine learning approaches. Rather than relying exclusively on manually programmed rules, researchers began designing algorithms capable of learning patterns directly from data. Statistical modelling, neural networks, evolutionary computation, fuzzy logic, probabilistic reasoning, and support vector machines expanded the capabilities of intelligent systems while improving adaptability, prediction accuracy, and decision-making performance. Significant improvements in computational hardware further accelerated AI research during this period. A landmark achievement occurred in 1997 when IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov, demonstrating the ability of intelligent computing systems to outperform human experts in highly specialized domains. This achievement attracted worldwide attention and illustrated the practical potential of Artificial Intelligence beyond theoretical research. Similar advances subsequently appeared in speech recognition, computer vision, autonomous robotics, medical diagnosis, financial forecasting, and industrial automation.The twenty-first century has witnessed unprecedented growth in Artificial Intelligence driven by three major technological developments: the availability of massive digital datasets, substantial improvements in computational processing power, and the emergence of advanced machine learning algorithms. The rapid expansion of the internet, cloud computing, mobile technologies, social media, and digital services generated enormous volumes of data that enabled intelligent systems to learn more effectively. Simultaneously, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), high-performance computing, and cloud-based infrastructure significantly accelerated AI model training and deployment across diverse application domains. Deep learning has become one of the most influential developments in contemporary Artificial Intelligence. Inspired by the structure of the human brain, deep neural networks consist of multiple computational layers capable of learning complex representations from large datasets. These architectures have dramatically improved performance in image recognition, speech processing, language translation, autonomous driving, medical imaging, recommendation systems, fraud detection, and scientific research. Deep learning has transformed Artificial Intelligence from narrow task-specific applications into highly sophisticated systems capable of addressing increasingly complex real-world challenges.Natural Language Processing (NLP) has experienced remarkable advancement through transformer architectures and large language models capable of understanding, generating, summarizing, translating, and analysing human language with unprecedented accuracy. Conversational AI systems, intelligent virtual assistants, multilingual communication platforms, automated content generation, and research support tools have become integral components of education, healthcare, business, governance, and scientific research. These developments have substantially enhanced human-computer interaction while expanding opportunities for intelligent educational technologies. The emergence of generative Artificial Intelligence represents another significant milestone in AI evolution. Modern generative models can produce text, images, computer code, audio, video, simulations, educational content, and scientific documentation while supporting creativity, innovation, research, and personalized learning. These technologies have transformed knowledge creation and digital communication by enabling collaborative interactions between humans and intelligent systems across numerous professional disciplines.Artificial Intelligence has evolved beyond isolated computational applications into a foundational technology supporting digital transformation across multiple sectors. Healthcare employs AI for disease diagnosis, medical imaging, drug discovery, personalized treatment, and patient monitoring. Manufacturing integrates AI with robotics, predictive maintenance, quality control, and smart production systems. Financial institutions utilize intelligent algorithms for fraud detection, risk management, investment analysis, and customer services. Agriculture benefits from precision farming, crop monitoring, environmental analysis, and resource optimization. Transportation increasingly relies upon autonomous vehicles, intelligent traffic management, and logistics optimization. Education has emerged as one of the fastest-growing application areas where Artificial Intelligence supports personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, curriculum development, learning analytics, educational administration, and lifelong learning. The evolution of Artificial Intelligence has also been closely associated with the progression from Industry 4.0 toward Industry 5.0. While Industry 4.0 emphasized automation, cyber-physical systems, and smart manufacturing, Industry 5.0 introduces a human-centred approach that balances technological innovation with creativity, ethics, sustainability, and social responsibility.
